books.section: Topic 5.9 Government Policies During the Civil War
Unit 5: Toward the Civil War and Reconstruction (1844–1877)

primary_sources: Abraham Lincoln, letter to Horace Greeley (August 22, 1862)

stimulus.source_note: Abraham Lincoln, letter to Horace Greeley, August 22, 1862. Public domain. Wording verified against the Collected Works text. “. . .” marks omitted text between passages, quoted in their order in the source.
stimulus.text:
“My paramount object in this struggle is to save the Union, and is not either to save or to destroy slavery. . . . I have here stated my purpose according to my view of official duty; and I intend no modification of my oft-expressed personal wish that all men everywhere could be free.”

—Abraham Lincoln, letter to Horace Greeley, August 22, 1862

source: original; stimulus as noted in stimulus.source_note
stem: Lincoln wrote this letter in August 1862, a month before he issued the preliminary Emancipation Proclamation. The letter best shows that Lincoln

options.text: had decided that slavery must be destroyed at once, whatever the cost to the Union.
options.misconception: Background: Lincoln says he would save the Union with or without freeing slaves; destroying slavery at any cost is the opposite of his stated position.

options.text: opposed emancipation and planned to leave slavery untouched for the rest of the war.
options.misconception: Background: a month later Lincoln issued the preliminary Emancipation Proclamation, so he was moving toward emancipation, not away from it.

options.text: believed the Constitution gave him no power over slavery anywhere in the country.
options.misconception: Background: Lincoln issued the proclamation as a war measure under his power as commander in chief.

options.text: was already moving toward emancipation but would defend it as a means to save the Union.

rationales.A: Background: Lincoln says he would save the Union with or without freeing slaves; destroying slavery at any cost is the opposite of his stated position.
rationales.B: Background: a month later Lincoln issued the preliminary Emancipation Proclamation, so he was moving toward emancipation, not away from it.
rationales.C: Background: Lincoln issued the proclamation as a war measure under his power as commander in chief.
rationales.D: The letter’s test is whether emancipation helps save the Union, and a month later Lincoln issued the preliminary proclamation on exactly those terms.
rationales.general:
1. Read the letter as a rule, not as a refusal: do about slavery whatever helps save the Union.
2. Then check the calendar: a month later Lincoln issues the preliminary proclamation.
3. Background: he had already drafted it and waited for a Union victory at Antietam.
4. The letter was his public frame for a step he was about to take.
Remember: a leader’s stated rule tells you what step comes next, and when.
